scenes.tts: Every day, in every one of your cells, some cytosines lose their amino group and turn into uracil. Uracil pairs with adenine, so the next replication puts an adenine opposite it. The round after that leaves an A T pair where a G C pair had been. That is a mutation made by chemistry alone. So how does a cell find a few wrong bases among billions of right ones?
scenes.visual: Three stacked duplexes of letter tiles. A G·C pair turns into U opposite G; replication puts A opposite U; the next round leaves an A·T pair, boxed as a mutation. Then one red tile among a long row of blue ones and a question mark.

scenes.tts: The answer lies in the double helix, which holds its information twice. If one strand is damaged, the cell cuts out the bad stretch and copies the partner strand. In base excision repair, a glycosylase flips the uracil out and cuts it from its sugar. Another enzyme nicks the backbone there, and a polymerase inserts the correct nucleotide, using the partner strand. A ligase seals the nick.
scenes.visual: A large duplex with a red U. A dome-shaped glycosylase takes the U out; the backbone is nicked; a polymerase puts a green C in, copied from the partner G; a ligase closes the nick.

scenes.tts: Ultraviolet light does bulkier damage. It joins two neighboring pyrimidines on one strand into a dimer that bends the helix. Nucleotide excision repair senses the bend, not the chemistry. It cuts the damaged strand on both sides and removes a short piece. A polymerase fills the gap from the partner strand, and a ligase seals it.
scenes.visual: UV waves hit two adjacent T tiles, which join in red and bend the strand. Cuts fall on both sides, the short piece lifts away, green tiles refill the gap, and the cuts are sealed.

scenes.tts: A mismatch is two normal bases paired wrongly, such as G with T. Neither is damaged, so the cell must find the new strand, because the template was correct. In E. coli, the template carries methyl groups at G A T C sites, and the new strand is briefly unmethylated. Mutt S binds the mismatch, Mutt L joins it, and Mutt H nicks the unmethylated strand. That strand is removed past the mismatch and rebuilt.
scenes.visual: A duplex with a red question mark between a G and a T. The strands are named template and new; methyl badges sit on the template GATC but not the new one. MutS, MutL, MutH arrive, the new strand is nicked, the stretch past the mismatch is removed and rebuilt in green.
scenes.caption: A mismatch is two normal bases paired wrongly, such as G with T. Neither is damaged, so the cell must find the new strand, because the template was correct. That strand is removed past the mismatch and rebuilt.

scenes.tts: A break through both strands removes the copying option at one spot. Picture a rope cut through. You can knot the ends, or splice in a matching length from an identical rope. Non-homologous end joining knots the ends: a ring-shaped protein, Ku, grips each end and a ligase joins them. It uses no template, so if the ends needed trimming, a few bases may be gained or lost.
scenes.visual: The duplex is cut through both strands and the copy arrow is crossed out. A cut rope (a drawn double helix) knots its ends, then a matching rope appears. Ku rings grip the two ends, which are joined with no template.

scenes.tts: Homologous recombination splices from a matching rope. Nucleases trim the ends to single-stranded tails, and Rad51 coats them and invades a matching duplex. The invading end primes synthesis, copying the information lost at the break. The best template is the sister chromatid, the identical copy made in replication. One rule runs through almost all repair: the information is held twice.
scenes.visual: A broken chromosome above its intact sister. Tails are trimmed, a coated tail invades the sister, green synthesis copies the lost stretch. A closing frame shows the helix with information held twice.
